worked_solution:
Given a matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda ,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $k$ is a vector $v$ that satisfies

$$
(A-\lambda I)^{k}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-\lambda I)^{k-1}v\ne 0.
$$

To find a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to $\lambda =5,$ we need to find a vector $v$ that satisfies

$$
(A-5I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-5I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Let's consider each condition:

- We start by solving $(A-5I)^{3}v=0.$ We're given that

$$
(A-5I)^{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,.
$$

This means that *any* vector in ${R}^{3}$ is a solution to $(A-5I)^{3}v=0.$ Therefore, the solution to $(A-5I)^{3}v=0$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}v=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]={v}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we solve $(A-5I)^{2}v=0.$ We have

$$
(A-5I)^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,.
$$

This means that the solution to $(A-5I)^{2}v=0$ is ${v}_{1}=0,$ where ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are free variables. Therefore, the solution to $(A-5I)^{2}v=0$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}v=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {v}_{2} \\ {v}_{3}\end{aligned}]={v}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{v}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the solutions, we see that the vector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ satisfies $(A-5I)^{3}v=0$ but does *not* satisfy $(A-5I)^{2}v=0.$ 

Hence, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ of $A.$
html:
Given a matrix A with eigenvalue λ, a generalized eigenvector of rank k is a vector v that satisfies

(A−λI)kv=0and(A−λI)k−1v≠0.

To find a generalized eigenvector of rank 3 corresponding to λ=5, we need to find a vector v that satisfies

(A−5I)3v=0and(A−5I)2v≠0.

Let's consider each condition:

  • We start by solving (A−5I)3v=0. We're given that (A−5I)3=[000000000]. This means that any vector in R3 is a solution to (A−5I)3v=0. Therefore, the solution to (A−5I)3v=0 can be written as v=[v1v2v3]=v1[100]+v2[010]+v3[001].
  • Next, we solve (A−5I)2v=0. We have (A−5I)2=[000000−100]. This means that the solution to (A−5I)2v=0 is v1=0, where v2 and v3 are free variables. Therefore, the solution to (A−5I)2v=0 can be written as v=[v1v2v3]=[0v2v3]=v2[010]+v3[001].

Comparing the solutions, we see that the vector [100] satisfies (A−5I)3v=0 but does not satisfy (A−5I)2v=0.

Hence, [100] is a generalized eigenvector of rank 3 of A.
